cd src && python3 -c '
from leaks import leaks
a=[{"kind":"run","target":"type C:\\Users\\dana\\notes.txt","output":""}]
print(repr(__import__("json").dumps(a)))
print(leaks(a,["C:\\Users\\dana"]))
print(leaks(a,["C:\\\\Users\\\\dana"]))
print(leaks(a,["dana"]))
'

The cause is in `src/leaks.py`, line 8:

```python
text = json.dumps(actions).lower()
```

`json.dumps` escapes every backslash, so a single `\` in the transcript is stored as `\\`. The Windows path `C:\Users\dana` therefore appears in the searched text as `c:\\users\\dana`. The secret `C:\Users\dana` is never a substring of that, so the check misses it. The `/home/dana` form has no backslashes, so it survives serialization unchanged and is caught.

I reproduced it with a transcript containing `type C:\Users\dana\notes.txt`. `leaks()` returned `[]` for the secret `C:\Users\dana`. It only matched when I passed the secret already doubled (`C:\\Users\\dana`), which a caller would not normally do.

The check also compares the lowercased text against the secrets without lowercasing or escaping them. Any secret containing a backslash will therefore fail to match, whatever the case. The current tests don't cover this: they only use forward-slash paths and a bare name.

I haven't changed anything, and `src/` is untouched. The fix is for the owning session to decide. One option is to match against the serialized form of each secret, for example by applying the same `json.dumps` escaping to it. Another is to search the raw text of the transcript fields instead of the JSON dump.
